notes.short: The tabernacle, “a copy and shadow” of heaven
notes.about: The place where the priests served is called “a copy and shadow of what is in heaven”. As a shadow shows a body's outline but not its substance, the tabernacle and its service showed in outline the true sanctuary where Christ ministers (verse 2), so it was built after the pattern God showed Moses.

figure.name: Type
figure.words: a copy and shadow of what is in heaven
figure.means: the tabernacle and its priestly service, which showed in outline the true sanctuary in heaven where Christ serves

original.note: In Greek “copy” is hupodeigma, a likeness, and “shadow” is skia, an outline with no substance of its own.

notes.evidence: Barnes says the tabernacle was a mere copy of heaven, a shadow beside the substance, its service the outline of a reality in heaven. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it a sketch of the heavenly sanctuary, the antitypical reality. Calvin says the Law's service was a picture to shadow forth what is found in Christ. Clarke calls it a representation and shadow of heavenly things.
notes.limit: One writer cautions against hunting for a deep meaning in every nail and small part of the tabernacle.

cites.quote: The reference is to the tabernacle, which was a mere "example" or "copy" of heaven. … Compared with what is in heaven, it was what the shadow is compared with the substance. … there exists in heaven a reality of which the service in the Jewish sanctuary was but the outline.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The Greek for "example" is here taken for the sketch, copy, or suggestive representation of the heavenly sanctuary, which is the antitypical reality and primary archetype.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: the Levitical priests, while exercising their functions, had nothing but a shadow and a copy … the whole service, according to the Law, was nothing more than a picture as it were, designed to shadow forth what is found spiritually in Christ. … There is, however, no reason that we should be here overcurious, so as to seek in every nail and minute things some sublime mystery
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The whole Levitical service was a representation and shadow of heavenly things
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The tabernacle as a picture of better things
notes.about: The tabernacle and its service, while the way into the Most Holy Place was not yet disclosed (9:8), are called an illustration. Its gifts and sacrifices could not cleanse the conscience. It pictured better things, found in Christ, “high priest of the good things that have come” (9:11).

figure.name: Type
figure.means: the tabernacle and its service, a picture of realities more fully shown later, which one writer says led worshipers to Christ

original.note: In Greek the word is parabole, literally a setting beside, the same word the Gospels use for a parable.

notes.evidence: Barnes says the word is not the one for type but the one commonly rendered parable, a placing side by side, and that the service as a whole was typical of things more fully revealed later. Clarke calls the whole a dark representation of a more glorious system. Calvin takes the word as antitype, a second pattern answering to the first, and says such symbols led the faithful by the hand to Christ.
notes.limit: The Greek word is not the usual word for a type, but the writers take the service it names as picturing what was to come. The note does not claim that every detail of the tabernacle points to something.

cites.quote: is not the same as type ... but is the word commonly rendered "parable;" ... means properly "a placing side by side;" ... the arrangements and services of the tabernacle were a representation of important realities, and of things which were more fully to be revealed at a future period. ... this service in general was symbolical or typical
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The whole was a figure, or dark representation, of a spiritual and more glorious system
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: signifies, as I think, the same thing with ἀντίτυπος, antitype; for he means that that tabernacle was a second pattern which corresponded with the first. ... for the faithful were by such helps led, as it were, by the hand to Christ, that they might obtain from him what was wanting in the symbols.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Goats and calves, set beside Christ's own blood
notes.about: Hebrews names the old offerings plainly: the blood of goats and calves, then the blood of goats and bulls. Set beside Christ's own blood, they look small, so that His one sacrifice is seen the greater: “how much more will the blood of Christ” purify our consciences (verse 14).

figure.name: Meiosis
figure.words: the blood of goats and calves
figure.means: the sacrifices under the Law, named plainly so that Christ's sacrifice of Himself is seen the greater

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists verses 12 and 13 under Meiosis: the figure lessens the sacrifices under the Law to increase by contrast the great sacrifice they pointed to. Calvin says the things of Christ so far excel the shadows of the Law as to reduce them all to nothing. Bengel says verse 13 confirms the power of Christ's one sacrifice, calls the bulls and goats mere brutes and names the figure Extenuation.
notes.limit: The note does not call the old offerings worthless: verse 13 says they made the body clean. One writer says they all pointed to Christ's great sacrifice; another calls them shadows that come to nothing beside the things of Christ.

cites.quote: “The blood of goats and calves,” (13) “the blood of bulls and of goats.” Here the figure lessens the importance of the sacrifices which were offered under the Law, in order to increase by contrast the great sacrifice to which they all pointed.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: All these things tend to show that the things of Christ so far excel the shadows of the Law, that they justly reduce them all to nothing. For what is the value of Christ’s blood, if it be deemed no better than the blood of beasts?
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: He confirms the fact, that the power of the one sacrifice of Christ is as great as he intimated at Hebrews 9:12. ... of bulls and goats, which are mere brutes. Extenuation.
cites.read: Bible Hub's transcription, at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/bengel/hebrews/9.htm

notes.short: The earthly holy place, a copy of heaven itself
notes.about: The holy place on earth is called “a man-made copy of the true sanctuary”. Its inner room pictured heaven, and the high priest's going in once a year pictured Christ, who has entered heaven itself “to appear on our behalf in the presence of God.”

figure.name: Type
figure.words: a man-made copy of the true sanctuary
figure.means: the earthly holy place, made after a heavenly pattern, which pictured heaven itself, where Christ now appears before God for us

original.note: In the Greek of Hebrews “copy” is antitypa: something shaped to match an original pattern.

notes.evidence: Barnes says the tabernacle was the type of heaven: its most holy place stood for heaven, the high priest's entering for Christ's. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls the holy places copies of heaven, the original. Calvin calls the old sanctuary the antitype of the true, its priest typical. Moulton (Ellicott's commentary) sets Christ in heaven against a priest before a symbol.

cites.quote: He has entered into the true temple - heaven - of which the earthly tabernacle was the type. … the most holy place denoted heaven; the mercy-seat and the shekinah were symbols of the presence of God, and of the fact that he shows mercy in heaven; the entrance of the high priest was emblematical of the entrance of the Redeemer into heaven
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: copies "of the true" holiest place, heaven, the original archetype … Aaron, the Levitical high priest for the people, stood before the ark and only saw the cloud, the symbol of God's glory
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He calls the old sanctuary the ἀντίτυπον, the antitype of the true, that is, of the spiritual; for all the external figures represented as in a mirror what would have otherwise been above our corporeal senses. … So formerly the Levitical priest stood before God in the name of the people, but typically; for in Christ is found the reality and the full accomplishment of what was typified.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

On the Day of Atonement the high priest came before what was but a symbol of the Divine Presence

notes.short: The law is “a shadow of the good things to come”
notes.about: The law with its yearly sacrifices is called a shadow of the good things to come: an outline that points ahead, “not the realities themselves.” So those sacrifices could never make the worshipers perfect, but Christ “by a single offering” has done so (10:14).

figure.name: Type
figure.words: a shadow of the good things to come
figure.means: the law and its sacrifices, an outline pointing ahead to the good things Christ brings, not the realities themselves

original.note: In the Greek of Hebrews the law has a skia, a shadow or first sketch, and not the eikon, the finished image of the things.

notes.evidence: Bullinger, under Type, says the theologians' sense of type agrees with the New Testament's shadow, citing this verse. Barnes calls the sacrifices a dim outline, a typical representation. Clarke sets the law, a shadow, against the Gospel, the thing itself. Calvin likens it to a painter's sketch of the same Christ. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it acted prophecy of Christ's offering.
notes.limit: Two of the writers read the shadow here as an artist's early sketch, not yet the finished picture.

cites.quote: The theological use of the word agrees more with what in the New Testament is called σκιά (skia), a shadow (Heb. x. 1. Col. ii. 17)
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The word "shadow" here refers to a rough outline of anything, a mere sketch ... such as an artist delineates when he is about to make a picture. ... The idea is, that under the ancient sacrifices there was an imperfect representation; a dim outline of the blessings which the gospel would impart to people. They were a typical representation
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The law, with all its ceremonies and sacrifices, was only a shadow of spiritual and eternal good. The Gospel is the image or thing itself, as including every spiritual and eternal good. ... such is Christ, when compared with Aaron; such is his sacrifice, when compared with the Levitical offerings
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He has borrowed this similitude from the pictorial art ... The difference then which the Apostle makes between the Law and the Gospel is this, — that under the Law was shadowed forth only in rude and imperfect lines what is under the Gospel set forth in living colors and graphically distinct. ... Hence to both the same Christ is exhibited, the same righteousness, sanctification, and salvation
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The law was a continual process of acted prophecy, proving the divine design that its counterparts should come; and proving the truth of those counterparts when they came. Thus the imperfect and continued expiatory sacrifices before Christ foretend, and now prove, the reality of, Christ's one perfect antitypical expiation.

notes.short: Their own losses around their care for others
notes.about: The first and last lines tell what they bore themselves: public ridicule and persecution, and the confiscation of their property, accepted with joy. The two lines between tell how they stood with others who suffered.

lines.words: Sometimes you were publicly exposed to ridicule and persecution;
at other times you were partners with those who were so treated.
You sympathized with those in prison
and joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property,

notes.evidence: Jebb calls the epanodos in these two verses indisputable. The leading object, how nobly they rose above their own afflictions and losses, begins and ends the stanza, in the first line and the fourth; a lesser point, their sympathy with the imprisoned apostle, is set in the central couplet.
notes.limit: Manuscripts differ in verse 34 on whom they sympathized with, those in prison or the writer in his chains; scholars differ.

cites.quote: In these two verses the epanodos is indisputable. … with how great personal magnanimity they had … risen superior to their own personal afflictions and deprivations; and with this, his leading object, he commences, and concludes, in the first line, and the fourth. A subordinate circumstance remained: their sympathy, namely, with S. Paul in his imprisonment. … in this central couplet
cites.read: the 1820 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/sacredliterature00jebb

notes.short: Isaac received back: a figure of rising
notes.about: Abraham gave Isaac up to death on the altar and received him back alive. The verse says this was so “in a sense,” that is, in a figure. Many read it as a picture pointing ahead to the rising of the dead; some see in it Christ's death and rising, the ram dying in Isaac's place.

figure.name: Type
figure.words: in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death
figure.means: Isaac received back alive from the altar, a picture pointing ahead to rising from the dead

original.note: In the Greek of Hebrews “in a sense” is en parabolē, literally “in a parable”, that is, in a figure.

notes.evidence: Barnes: Isaac, raised from the altar as if from the grave, was to Abraham a figure of the resurrection. Benson: a resemblance of the resurrection, the deliverance a type of it, the whole an apt emblem of the sacrifice of the Son of God. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) reads the scene as Christ's death, the ram in Isaac's stead, and His rising.
notes.limit: Writers differ on what the figure points to: the rising of the dead, or Christ slain and raised.

cites.quote: From that altar he was raised up by direct divine interposition, as if he was raised from the grave, and this was to Abraham a "figure" or a representation of the resurrection.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: From whence also he received him in a figure That is, Figuratively speaking, or in a figure or resemblance of the resurrection from the dead, as being hindered from slaying him. … the miraculous birth of Isaac was not so proper a type of a resurrection as his deliverance from death was … Abraham's offering up Isaac will appear to be a most apt emblem of the sacrifice of the Son of God.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: understanding the figure to be the representation which the whole scene gave to Abraham of Christ in His death (typified by Isaac's offering in intention, and the ram's actual substitution answering to Christ's vicarious death), and in His resurrection … he received him back as a type of the resurrection in Christ.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: “Of no advantage” says far less than it means
notes.about: If the leaders must lead with grief, the verse says, “that would be of no advantage to you.” The mild words say far less than is meant. The writers read them as real harm to the hearers themselves, and some as a danger to their very souls.

figure.name: Meiosis
figure.means: not merely no gain, but real harm to the hearers, even to their souls

original.note: In the Greek of Hebrews, “of no advantage” is one word, alusitelēs, unprofitable.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Meiosis, a belittling, and says the harm meant is far greater, even ruin. Barnes reads the words as not of advantage but highly injurious, a strong way of saying their souls would be in great peril. Bengel says the leaders' sighs would not profit the hearers but greatly harm them. Calvin says the words hint that troubling our pastors puts our own salvation at risk.
notes.limit: The writers explain the harm in different ways: leaders worn down by grief, or an account given against the hearers when the leaders answer to God.

cites.quote: “For that is unprofitable for you.” It is really much more than that! It is disastrous and ruinous.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: would not be of advantage to you, but would be highly injurious. This is a strong mode of expressing the idea that it must be attended with eminent peril to their souls to have their religious teachers go and give an account against them.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: greatly weakens the teachers; and their sighs are not profitable, nay, are very injurious to the disciples.
cites.read: Bible Hub's transcription, at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/bengel/hebrews/13.htm

cites.quote: Hence the Apostle declares, that it would be unprofitable to the people to cause sorrow and mourning to their pastors by their ingratitude; and he did this, that he might intimate to us that we cannot be troublesome or disobedient to our pastors without hazarding our own salvation.
